# Karnataka EV Policy Explained: What It Means for EV Charging Infrastructure

As EV adoption accelerates, the limiting factor is no longer vehicle availability but the infrastructure required to support it.

State policies are increasingly shaping how EV ecosystems evolve, particularly in areas such as charging access, grid readiness, and private sector participation.

Among Indian states, Karnataka stands out as an early mover that has consistently aligned policy with ecosystem development. For EV infrastructure players, the Karnataka EV Policy offers a clear signal of where the market is heading and how charging networks are expected to scale.

## TL;DR

## Karnataka EV Policy Highlights

* The state transition to the Clean Mobility Policy 2025–30, targeting ₹50,000 crore in investments by 2030.
* Capital incentives ranging from 20% to 35% for MSMEs and up to 25% for large enterprises.
* Plans to add 2,500 new charging stations via Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) and charging points every 60–70 km on state highways.
* Karnataka rolled back the 100% road tax exemption in 2026; new lifetime taxes range from 5% to 10% based on vehicle cost.
* Allocation of ₹3,400 crore for Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to support the grid during peak EV demand.
* Establishment of dedicated mobility clusters in Gauribidanur, Dharwad, and Harohalli.

## **What is Karnataka EV Policy?**

The Karnataka EV Policy is a regulatory and incentive framework designed to promote electric mobility by supporting:

* EV manufacturing

* EV adoption

* Charging infrastructure deployment

## **Overview of Karnataka EV Policy**

Karnataka, recognized as the first Indian state to launch a dedicated electric vehicle (EV) policy in 2017, strengthened the framework in 2021 to improve investor economics, and expanded it again on February 11, 2025, through the**Clean Mobility Policy 2025–30**.

### **Objectives and Vision**

The primary vision is to attract **₹500 billion (₹50,000 crore)** in investment by 2030 and create a sustainable, multi-modal transport system. The policy envisions:

* **100% electrification** of public transport and government fleets by 2030

* Generating high-value employment across the EV supply chain

* Fostering innovation in **hydrogen fuel cell** technology alongside battery electric vehicles (BEVs)

### **Key Incentives for Manufacturers and Consumers**

The [Karnataka Clean Mobility Policy 2025–2030](https://investkarnataka.co.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Government-of-Karnataka-Unveils-Clean-Mobility-Policy.pdf), alongside the 2026 Taxation Amendment, establishes a balanced ecosystem. While the state is moving toward a revenue-generating model for high-end vehicles, it remains one of the most aggressive Indian states in subsidizing manufacturing and infrastructure.

**1. For Manufacturers: Boosting the Supply Chain**

To cement its status as a global EV hub, Karnataka offers heavy capital subsidies and operational cost waivers, particularly focusing on MSMEs and R&D.

| **Category** | **Capital Subsidy (on Fixed Assets)** | **Maximum Cap** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Micro Industries** | 20% to 35% | ₹3.5 Million |
| **Small Enterprises** | 20% to 30% | ₹22.5 Million |
| **Medium Enterprises** | 20% to 25% | ₹100 Million |
| **R&D Projects** | 30% Reimbursement of costs | ₹10 Million |

**Operational Perks for Industry:**

* **Tax Exemptions:** A [100% exemption](https://www.evsahihai.com/policies/karnataka-policy#:~:text=Capital%20Subsidy%20of%2025%25%20on,5%2C00%2C000%20per%20station.) on electricity Duty for the initial 5 years (depending on the industrial zone).

* **Land Benefits:** A [100% reimbursement](https://mobiintel.com/karnataka-clean-mobility-policy-2025-30-driving-the-future-of-sustainable-transport/#:~:text=Sustainable%20Transport%20%E2%80%93%20Mobiintel-,Karnataka%20Clean%20Mobility%20Policy%202025%2D30:%20Driving,the%20Future%20of%20Sustainable%20Transport&text=Karnataka%20has%20taken%20a%20bold,benefits%20of%20this%20futuristic%20initiative.&text=The%20Karnataka%20government%20envisions:,Asia's%20top%20clean%20mobility%20hub) of land conversion fee and full exemption from stamp duty on lease or sale of land.

* **EV Clusters:** Special incentives for units set up in designated clusters like **Dharwad** and **Gauribidanur**.

**2. For Consumers: The New Taxation Era**

Effective April 1, 2026, [Karnataka](https://dpal.karnataka.gov.in/uploads/media_to_upload1776323794.pdf) transitioned from a “zero-tax” regime to a tiered Lifetime Tax (LTT) for electric four-wheelers. Budget EVs remain accessible while luxury models contribute more to infrastructure funds.

| **Vehicle Type** | **Price Bracket** | **Lifetime Road Tax** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Two-Wheelers** | All Prices | **0% (Fully Exempt)** |
| **Electric Cars/Jeeps** | Under ₹10 Lakh | 5% |
|  | ₹10 Lakh – ₹25 Lakh | 8% |
|  | Above ₹25 Lakh | 10% |

Additional Consumer Benefits:

* **Fast Charging Subsidy:** A [25%](https://www.mercomindia.com/karnatakas-clean-mobility-policy-2025-30-targets-%E2%82%B9500-billion-investment) capital subsidy (up to ₹10 lakh) for the first 500 public charging stations.

* **Battery Swapping:** 25% subsidy for swapping stations, capped at ₹3 lakh for 2-wheeler networks and ₹10 lakh for bus networks.

* **Commercial Permits:** [Zero-fee](https://www.moneycontrol.com/news/india/karnataka-mandates-zero-fee-permits-for-electric-green-commercial-vehicles-13220195.html) permits for commercial electric and green vehicles

## **Infrastructure Development Plans**

 

A core pillar of the **Karnataka electric vehicle policy** is the rapid expansion of the charging network to eliminate “range anxiety” for long-distance travelers.

### **Charging Stations and Grid Readiness**

The state has moved beyond urban-centric charging to a corridor approach.

* The Bangalore Electricity Supply Company (BESCOM) and Karnataka Road Development Corporation Limited (KRDCL) are installing fast chargers every **60–70 km** at toll plazas, bus bays, and truck laybys.

* The 2024-25 budget allocated **₹350 million** to establish [**2,500 new stations**](https://www.mercomindia.com/karnatakas-clean-mobility-policy-2025-30-targets-%E2%82%B9500-billion-investment) under a public-private partnership (PPP) model.
* To handle demand, Karnataka is investing [**₹3,400 crore**](https://www.eqmagpro.com/indias-energy-storage-sector-accelerates-in-2025-amid-surge-in-bess-tenders-eq/) in **Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS),** ensuring excess solar energy can be used for EV charging at night without straining the grid.

## **Impact on EV Adoption in Karnataka**

The **EV policy Karnataka 2026** landscape shows a maturing market. While the rollback of road tax exemptions suggests fiscal sustainability, [the state continues to lead in “charging density”.](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/bengaluru/ktaka-plans-ev-charging-points-every-60-70km-on-state-highways/articleshow/130063308.cms)

### **Opportunities for Businesses**

For stakeholders in the **EV ecosystem India**, Karnataka offers unique advantages:

1. Stacking incentives from the EV policy with the **ESDM (Electronics System Design and Manufacturing)** policy allows MSMEs to [reduce CAPEX by 40–60%.](https://www.kredx.com/blog/karnataka-esdm-incentives-2025-203/)

1. The policy mandates a percentage of parking in cities for clean-fuel vehicles, creating a “push” for e-commerce and delivery companies to electrify fleets.

1. Charge Point Operators (CPOs) benefit from a [**25%**](https://www.mercomindia.com/karnatakas-clean-mobility-policy-2025-30-targets-%E2%82%B9500-billion-investment)**capital subsidy** (up to ₹10 lakh) for the first 500 fast-charging stations.

## **Final Thoughts**

The Karnataka EV policy story is now bigger than EVs alone. It spans manufacturing, charging, grid readiness, land use, skills, and clean mobility clusters. This makes the state one of India’s most important policy labs for companies operating across **EV ecosystem India**. Long-term winners will be businesses that align with infrastructure density, fast-charging access, and the new economics of clean mobility.

 

## Frequently Asked Questions

### **What is the latest Karnataka EV policy?**  Karnataka’s latest major framework is the Clean Mobility Policy 2025–30, which extends the state’s EV push beyond vehicles into charging, hydrogen, battery recycling, testing, and manufacturing.

### **Is there still a road tax exemption for EVs in Karnataka in 2026?**

No.

The 100% exemption was rolled back in 2026. EVs are now taxed based on price: 5% for vehicles under ₹10 lakh, 8% for ₹10–25 lakh, and 10% for luxury EVs above ₹25 lakh.

### **Can private sector employees in Karnataka get BH (Bharat) Series registration for EVs to avoid high state taxes?**

This remains a grey area. While the Karnataka High Court ruled in favor of private employees (working in companies with offices in 4+ states) getting BH series, RTO have resisted implementation.

As of 2026, while the option exists on paper, many dealers still struggle to process it. If one successfully gets a BH plate, they pay tax in two-year increments at a centralized rate, which is significantly lower than Karnataka’s 8–10% upfront lifetime tax.

### **Is an EV still worth it in Karnataka now that the 0% tax is gone?**

Yes.

Despite the **5–10% road tax,** the “Total Cost of Ownership” (TCO) still favors EVs.

For a mid-range SUV (like a Nexon EV or XUV400), the upfront tax adds up to ₹1.2–1.6 lakh, but lower running costs (~₹1.4/km vs. ~₹7-9/km for petrol) offset within 18–24 months.

# Do You Need a Driving Licence for an Electric Scooter in India? 2026 Rules Explained

Some electric two-wheelers legally need no licence and no registration. Almost none of the ones you actually want to buy fall in that group. Here is the 2026 rulebook — thresholds, licence classes, RC and Vahan, HSRP and green plates, state road tax, IRDAI insurance rates, helmet law and penalties — with sources.

Published On 29 Jul 2026, 4:46 pm•By MeraEV Bike Editorial Team

15 min

Share:

[Write a comment](#comments)

![Do You Need a Driving Licence for an Electric Scooter in India? 2026 Rules Explained](https://ik.imagekit.io/meraev/tr:w-1000,f-auto,q-60/blogs/driving-licence-electric-scooter-india-rules-2026/ChatGPT_Image_Jul_29__2026__11_30_54_AM__kCpFTw-s.png)

Ask three showrooms in the same city whether the scooter on the floor needs a licence and you may get three answers.

The confusion is understandable. India does have a genuine exemption for very slow, very low-powered electric two-wheelers, written into how the Motor Vehicles Act and the Central Motor Vehicles Rules define a motor vehicle at all. It is narrow, and plenty of products are sold with claims that quietly stretch it. Here is what the law says as of 29 July 2026. Rules change often and several are state subjects, so confirm anything affecting a purchase or a challan with your RTO first.

## The short answer

If the motor is rated above 250 watts, or the maximum speed is above 25 km/h, the vehicle is a motor vehicle: driving licence, RTO registration, an RC, a number plate and at least third-party insurance. There is no softer rulebook for EVs.

Below both thresholds, it is not a motor vehicle, and neither applies. Every scooter a mainstream buyer shortlists — Ather 450 and Rizta, Ola S1, TVS iQube, Bajaj Chetak, Hero Vida — sits on the regulated side of that line.

## The 250-watt, 25 km/h line that decides everything

Electric two-wheelers with a motor output of up to 250 W and a maximum speed of up to 25 km/h are exempt from type approval, registration and licensing. EVreporter, which tracks homologation for the Indian EV sector, attributes this to MoRTH notification G.S.R. 291(E), noting that e-2Ws "having maximum power less than 250 W and speed less than 25 kmph are exempt from type approval requirements".

Autocar India, reporting on a government review of the category, adds a third condition most buyers never hear about: e-2Ws "that remain within the 250W motor output, 60kg unladen weight and 25kph top-speed thresholds are treated as non-motor vehicles" under CMVR. All three must hold.

### Why the exemption is smaller than it sounds

A 250 W motor is roughly a third of a horsepower. It moves a rider on flat ground at cycling speed and struggles on a flyover with a pillion. The exemption exists for a powered bicycle, not a scooter.

This is where the market gets messy. EVreporter has documented CMVR and consumer-protection concerns around low-speed models sold with performance beyond the exempt limits — which makes them unregistered motor vehicles the moment they leave the showroom. If a dealer says a scooter needs no registration but quotes a 45 km/h top speed, both claims cannot be true. Ask whether it has ARAI or ICAT type approval.

| Requirement | Low-speed e-2W (≤250 W, ≤25 km/h) | High-speed e-2W (above either threshold) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Driving licence | Not required | Required |
| RTO registration and RC | Not required | Mandatory |
| Number plate | Not issued | Green HSRP mandatory |
| Motor insurance | Not mandatory under the MV Act | Third-party cover mandatory |
| Road tax | Not applicable | Applicable, subject to state exemptions |
| Type approval (ARAI/ICAT) | Exempt | Mandatory |
| Minimum rider age | No statutory MV Act age | 18 years (16 in a narrow case) |
| Helmet under Section 129 | Not covered by the section | Mandatory for rider and pillion |
| Typical use case | Short, low-speed neighbourhood runs | Daily commuting, highways, pillion duty |

## Which licence class covers an electric scooter

Licence classes are written around the vehicle, not the fuel. Almost every electric scooter sold here is a twist-and-go, single-speed machine with no clutch and no gear lever, which places it under the gearless motorcycle class — printed on licences as M/CYCL.WOG or MCWOG. MCWG, the geared class, covers gearless two-wheelers as well. Only multi-speed electric motorcycles need the geared class.

### Minimum age, and the 16-to-17 question

Section 4(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 governs: "No person under the age of eighteen years shall drive a motor vehicle in any public place." Its proviso allows one exception — "a motor cycle with engine capacity not exceeding 50cc may be driven in a public place by a person after attaining the age of sixteen years."

The difficulty is that Section 4(1) is written in cubic centimetres, a unit that does not exist on an electric scooter. Several insurer and dealer explainers circulate a figure of 4 kW and 70 km/h as the electric equivalent for 16- and 17-year-olds; we could not trace it to any gazette notification or CMVR amendment. On a notified cc-to-kilowatt equivalence for the proviso: Official information has not yet been released.

RTOs therefore handle this inconsistently. If you are buying for a teenager, settle it at the counter before you pay. Otherwise the rule is 18 years.

### Learner's licence, then permanent licence

The route is identical to a petrol scooter. Apply on Parivahan Sarathi, clear the online test on road signs and rules, then ride with L-plates and no pillion. A learner's licence is valid for six months, and the permanent test comes after a prescribed waiting period and before it expires.

| Step | What you do | Who does it | Typical timeline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Learner's licence application | Apply on Parivahan Sarathi with Aadhaar, address and age proof | Buyer | 1 day (online test) |
| Learner's licence issued | Valid 6 months, L-plates, no pillion | RTO | Same day to a few days |
| Permanent licence test | Riding test at RTO or authorised centre | Buyer | After the prescribed waiting period |
| Vehicle invoice and Form 20 | Purchase documents and registration application | Dealer | At booking or delivery |
| Temporary registration | Temporary mark, valid up to one month | Dealer/RTO | At delivery, if applicable |
| Permanent registration on Vahan | Chassis and motor details, insurance, address proof | Dealer, on Vahan | Days to a few weeks |
| RC issued | Digital RC on DigiLocker/mParivahan, card by post | RTO | Varies by state |
| HSRP green plate fitted | Green plate with laser-etched PIN and hologram | Dealer/authorised vendor | At or shortly after delivery |
| Insurance in force | Five-year third-party cover for a new two-wheeler | Dealer/insurer | Before the vehicle is used |

## Registration, RC and Vahan

Registration is required under Section 39 of the Motor Vehicles Act, but buyers rarely deal with the RTO directly. Dealers are onboarded onto Vahan and complete dealer-point registration for you, uploading the sale invoice, Form 20, insurance details, chassis and motor numbers, and your address proof.

Temporary registration under Section 43 covers vehicles that must move before permanent registration is complete, and is valid generally for not more than one month.

A new non-transport two-wheeler receives an RC valid for 15 years, renewable thereafter in five-year blocks. It is available through DigiLocker and mParivahan, and a digital RC is legally valid during a check.

Do not take delivery without a registration mark in place — riding home unregistered is an offence, and the dealer's convenience is not a defence.

## HSRP and the green number plate

High Security Registration Plates come from an amendment to Rule 50 of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989. They are aluminium, non-reusable, snap-locked, and carry a chromium hologram and a laser-etched identification number. They have been mandatory on new vehicles sold in India since 1 April 2019, fitted at the dealer end.

Battery-operated vehicles get a green background rather than white or yellow. Private EVs carry white characters on green; commercial and transport EVs carry yellow. That is what every RTO and plate vendor applies, and what Autocar India reported when the measure was announced in 2018.

On the exact gazette number of the EV-specific amendment to Rule 50: Official information has not yet been released in a form we could verify, so we have described the scheme rather than quote a citation we cannot stand behind. The plate is not decorative — it is how enforcement, tolling and several state incentive schemes identify an EV.

## Road tax and registration fee exemptions

Two things get confused here. Registration fees are central: through notification G.S.R. 525(E) dated 2 August 2021, MoRTH exempted battery-operated vehicles nationwide from fees for issue or renewal of a registration certificate and for assignment of a new registration mark.

Road tax is not. States levy it under their own Motor Vehicles Taxation Acts, each setting its own exemption percentage and sunset date. This is where the most out-of-date advice circulates, because state policies have been expiring and being rewritten through 2025 and 2026. The table below is indicative — confirm the rate with your RTO before you book.

| State / UT | Indicative road tax position for electric two-wheelers | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Delhi | Full exemption reported | Confirm current policy status |
| Maharashtra | Full exemption reported | Under the 2021 EV policy framework |
| Karnataka | Two-wheelers reported to remain exempt | Tiered lifetime tax introduced for larger EVs from April 2026 |
| Uttar Pradesh | Full exemption reported | Tied to state EV policy period |
| Rajasthan | Full exemption reported | Confirm current policy status |
| Punjab | Full exemption reported | Confirm current policy status |
| Odisha | Full exemption reported | Confirm current policy status |
| Tamil Nadu | Exemption reported with a stated end date | Verify the applicable cut-off |
| Telangana | Exemption reported with a stated end date | Verify the applicable cut-off |
| Madhya Pradesh | Reduced rate reported after exemption lapse | Verify current slab |
| Gujarat | Concessional rate reported, subject to policy expiry | Verify whether the concession is still live |
| Haryana | Exemption reported to be capped by registration volume | Quota may be exhausted |

Karnataka shows why. Reporting on the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Taxation (Amendment) Bill, 2026 indicates a tiered lifetime tax on higher-value electric four-wheelers from 1 April 2026, with two-wheelers left exempt. Policies move; the RTO counter is the only authority on what you will pay.

### The PM E-Drive deadline

Under PM E-Drive, the Ministry of Heavy Industries set the e-2W demand incentive at ₹2,500 per kWh, capped at ₹5,000 per vehicle, from 1 April 2025. Autocar India reported in March 2026 that the window was extended to 31 July 2026, four months past the original cut-off. We are not aware of any further extension having been notified. If your quotation shows a price net of this incentive, ask the dealer to confirm in writing that it applies to your delivery date.

## Insurance: what is mandatory and what it costs

Third-party liability cover is mandatory for every motor vehicle used in a public place under Section 146 of the Motor Vehicles Act. There is no EV exemption. Own-damage cover is optional but sensible when the battery pack is the most expensive component.

Third-party rates are notified centrally and identical across insurers. For electric two-wheelers they are set by motor power in kilowatts, and the EV slabs already reflect a 15 per cent concession against comparable petrol categories.

| Electric two-wheeler category | Third-party premium |
| --- | --- |
| Not exceeding 3 kW | ₹457 |
| Exceeding 3 kW but not exceeding 7 kW | ₹607 |
| Exceeding 7 kW but not exceeding 16 kW | ₹1,161 |
| Exceeding 16 kW | ₹2,383 |

These rates were notified for FY 2022-23, effective 1 June 2022, and have not been revised since. One rule catches new buyers: since 1 September 2018, following a Supreme Court direction implemented through IRDAI circular IRDAI/NUCIR/MOTA31108/2018 dated 28 August 2018, a new two-wheeler must be sold with five-year third-party cover.

## Helmets

Section 129 of the Motor Vehicles Act requires protective headgear conforming to Bureau of Indian Standards specifications for anyone riding or being carried on a two-wheeler. It applies to the pillion as much as the rider. Sikhs wearing a turban are exempted under the section.

The standard is IS 4151:2015. Under the Helmet for riders of Two Wheeler Motor Vehicles (Quality Control) Order, 2020, notified by MoRTH on 26 November 2020 and in force from 1 June 2021, helmets sold in India must carry BIS certification against it. An imported lid with only a foreign mark does not satisfy the requirement.

## PUC, fitness certificate and paperwork you do not need

A Pollution Under Control certificate certifies tailpipe emissions. A battery electric scooter has no tailpipe and nothing to measure, so testing centres cannot test one and RTOs do not issue PUCCs for them. EV owners are not required to carry one.

Enforcement is not always aligned with that — EV owners have received pollution e-challans in error, a Gurugram case in November 2025 drawing wide attention. Contest it on the Parivahan e-challan portal with your RC showing the fuel type as electric.

Fitness certificates are a transport-vehicle requirement. A privately registered electric scooter does not need one during the 15-year validity of its RC.

## What happens if you ride an unregistered high-speed e-scooter

The Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 raised penalties sharply, and they apply to electric two-wheelers exactly as to petrol.

| Offence | Section | Penalty |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Driving without a valid licence | 181 | ₹5,000 |
| Using a vehicle without registration | 192 | ₹5,000 first offence; up to ₹10,000 for a subsequent offence |
| Driving without insurance | 196 | ₹2,000 first offence; ₹4,000 subsequent |
| Riding without a helmet (rider or pillion) | 194D | ₹1,000 plus licence disqualification for three months |
| Offence by a juvenile | 199A | Guardian or owner deemed guilty; fine up to ₹25,000 with imprisonment up to three years; vehicle registration cancelled for twelve months; juvenile ineligible for a licence until age 25 |
| General offence | 177 | ₹500 first offence; ₹1,500 subsequent |

Section 199A deserves a second read in any household with a teenager. Liability lands on the guardian or registered owner, the vehicle's registration is cancelled for a year, and the young rider cannot hold a licence until 25.

## Expert Insights

The regulatory risk is not with mainstream brands. Ather, Ola, TVS, Bajaj and Hero all sell type-approved vehicles, and their dealers complete Vahan registration as routine. The risk sits in the low-speed segment, where 250 W and 25 km/h are a real engineering constraint that some products meet on paper and not on the road.

There is also a resale dimension that rarely comes up at the point of sale. An unregistered vehicle has no RC — no formal transfer of ownership, no loan against it, no straightforward insurance claim, a thin second-hand market. Buyers who pick a low-speed model to skip paperwork often discover the cost of that two years later.

Note where the moving parts are. Central rules are stable and uniform. State rules on road tax and incentives are neither.

## Pros and Cons: low-speed versus high-speed ownership

### Low-speed electric two-wheeler

**Pros:** No licence, registration, road tax or mandatory insurance premium. Lower purchase price. Fine for very short local trips.

**Cons:** A 25 km/h ceiling is unsuitable for most Indian commuting. No RC, so no clean ownership transfer and weak resale. No insurance protection by default. A real risk of buying a product marketed as exempt that does not meet all three conditions.

### High-speed electric scooter

**Pros:** Usable in real traffic, on flyovers and with a pillion. Full legal standing — RC, green HSRP, insurance, transferable ownership. Eligible for state road-tax exemptions.

**Cons:** Licence, registration and insurance are mandatory and add cost and time. Penalties are severe if any lapses, and shifting state incentives make on-road prices less predictable.

## Common myths, debunked

**"No EV needs a licence in India."** False. Only vehicles at or below 250 W and 25 km/h fall outside the motor vehicle definition.

**"Anything under 25 km/h is exempt, whatever the motor."** False. Both conditions must hold, plus a reported 60 kg weight limit.

**"EVs don't need insurance."** False. Third-party cover under Section 146 applies to all motor vehicles.

**"EVs need a PUC like any other vehicle."** False in substance. There are no emissions to test and RTOs do not issue PUCCs, though enforcement errors happen.

## FAQs

### Do I need a driving licence for an electric scooter in India?

Yes, if the motor exceeds 250 W or the maximum speed exceeds 25 km/h. Such vehicles need a licence, registration and insurance. Only low-speed models below both thresholds are exempt.

### Which licence class do I need for an electric scooter?

For a typical twist-and-go scooter, the gearless class — printed as M/CYCL.WOG or MCWOG. MCWG, the geared class, covers gearless two-wheelers as well.

### Can a 16-year-old ride an electric scooter legally?

Section 4(1) permits a person aged 16 or above to drive a motor cycle not exceeding 50cc. Because electric motors are rated in kilowatts, the equivalence is unclear and RTOs treat it inconsistently. On a notified equivalence: Official information has not yet been released.

### What colour number plate does an electric scooter get?

A green plate — white characters for private EVs, yellow for commercial. It must be a High Security Registration Plate, mandatory on new vehicles since 1 April 2019.

### Is road tax waived on electric scooters?

Registration fees are exempt nationwide under notification G.S.R. 525(E) dated 2 August 2021. Road tax is a state subject — some states exempt fully, some partially, some not at all.

### How much is third-party insurance for an electric scooter?

Rates are set by motor power: ₹457 up to 3 kW, ₹607 for 3-7 kW, ₹1,161 for 7-16 kW and ₹2,383 above 16 kW, notified for FY 2022-23 and unrevised since. New two-wheelers need five-year cover.

### Do electric scooters need a PUC certificate?

No. A battery electric vehicle has no tailpipe emissions to measure and RTOs do not issue PUCCs. Challans issued in error can be contested on the Parivahan portal.

### Is a helmet mandatory for the pillion too?

Yes. Section 129 covers anyone riding or being carried on a two-wheeler and requires BIS-conforming headgear — IS 4151:2015, under the Quality Control Order in force since 1 June 2021. The Section 194D penalty is ₹1,000 plus three months' disqualification.

### What is the fine for riding an unregistered electric scooter?

₹5,000 for a first offence under Section 192, up to ₹10,000 for a subsequent one. Riding without a licence adds ₹5,000 under Section 181, and no insurance ₹2,000 under Section 196.

## Conclusion

The rules are not complicated once the threshold is clear. Above 250 watts or 25 km/h, an electric two-wheeler is a motor vehicle, and every obligation that applies to a petrol scooter applies to it. Below both thresholds, none do. What changes often is the layer around that — state road tax, subsidy windows, incentive deadlines. Treat this guide as your map of the fixed points and your RTO as the authority on the moving ones.

Concentrating all elements of the Clean Mobility Vehicle value chain, including OEMs and suppliers, within a single geographic location is essential. This approach serves to expedite research, innovation, and development, while also optimizing supply chain operations and fostering collaboration. Thus, the state Government is dedicated to promoting the formation of Clean Mobility clusters through PPP and aim to stimulate progress in Clean Mobility Vehicle technology, encourage economic advancement, and contribute to a more sustainable future in transportation. The pre-built factory/sheds would provide a head start to manufacturing operations, reducing initial setup time and costs. 4.2.2 Plug & Play incubation facility The plug-and-play incubation facility would serve as an innovation hub, offering a conducive environment for startups and emerging players to develop and refine their vehicle-related projects. These facilities would be equipped with essential infrastructure and services, ensuring that innovators can focus on their work without logistical hindrances. 4.2.3 Testing labs and Proving Grounds Indoor testing laboratories would be designed to facilitate research, development, and quality control processes, fostering precision and efficiency in Clean Mobility Vehicle manufacturing. The proving grounds and testing tracks would offer a real-world simulation environment for rigorous testing and validation of Clean Mobility Vehicle prototypes and components. 4.2.4 Homologation Facility The dedicated homologation facility within the state in one or more of the Clean Mobility Vehicle clusters would ensure that the manufactured Clean Mobility Vehicles meet stringent regulatory standards and quality benchmarks. # Primer Indian Laws Related To Electric Vehicles

Posted On - 17 February, 2025

The Indian Government is looking to develop and deploy more electric vehicles (“EVs”) on road by 2030 as a cost eﬀective and viable solution to the problem of poor air quality and huge oil import bills. NITI Aayog – India’s policy think tank, forecasts India’s EV sales penetration to reach 30% for private cars, 70% for commercial cars, 40% for buses and 80% for two and three-wheelers by 2030. Some of the common queries on laws applicable to EVs in India are answered below.

1. **What are the Indian laws related to EVs in India?**Currently, India does not have a dedicated law on EVs. In India, the law related to registration of motor vehicles, that is, the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 framed thereunder, provide for registration of EVs. Further, the Indian Government has published the ‘Model building bye-laws for EV charging infrastructure, 2016’ (“EV Bye-Laws”) which sets the guidelines to set up charging stations for EVs across the country. Indian states have also adopted state level policies to provide incentives to boost EVs.
2. **Are there any special concessions for EVs under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988?**The Indian Government has permitted sale and registration of EVs without a pre-fitted battery. Such EVs will require a road-worthiness approval from test agencies under the Central Motor Vehicle Rules, 1989. By delinking the cost of the battery (which accounts for 30-40% of the total cost) from the vehicle cost, EVs can now also be sold in the market without the battery. This will assist electrical 2-wheelers and 3-wheelers achieve cost parity with internal combustion engines.
3. **Who can set-up a public charging infrastructure as per the EV Bye-Laws?**No license is required to be obtained by a person for setting up of public charging station if the public charging station meets the technical and performance standards laid down by the Ministry of Power (“MoP”) and the Central Electricity Authority (“CEA”) further detailed in FAQ no. 4 below. Any person seeking to set up a public charging station may apply for connectivity to a power distribution company licensee. In this case, the power distribution company licensee is required to provide the connectivity to EV charging stations on priority. Alternatively, charging stations/ chains of charging stations may also purchase electricity directly from a power generation company at a lower tariff, without approaching a power distribution company.
4. **What are the minimum technical and performance standards required to be satisfied so that the EV public charging station can be set up without a license?**Currently, the minimum infrastructure requirements for EV public charging stations to be set up without a license are as follows:  
   (i) The station should have an exclusive transformer with all related substation equipment including safety appliance.  
   (ii) The station must use 33/11 KV line /cables with associated equipment, as may be needed for line termination /metering, etc.  
   (iii) The station must have appropriate civil works.  
   (iv) The station must have adequate space for charging and entry/exit of vehicles.  
   (v) Public charging stations must have one or more electric kiosk/boards with installation of at least one charging point and one charging gun of the CCS, the CHAdeMO, the Type-2 AC and the Bharat DC-001 variety, which are fast or semi-fast chargers. The charging station must also have three charging points and three charging guns of the Bharat AC-001 variety, which is a slow charger.  
   (vi) The station must have a tie up with at least one online Network Service Provider to enable advance remote/ online booking of charging slots by EV owners. Such online information to EV owners should also include information regarding location, types and numbers of chargers installed.  
   (vii) The station is required to share charging station data with appropriate power distribution company and to maintain appropriate protocols as prescribed by such power distribution company for this purpose.
5. **Is there a certification standard for EV batteries prescribed by the Indian Government?**In India, the Bureau of Indian Standards (“BIS”) pursuant to the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 has prescribed mandatory product standards for specified products such as electronics, cement, batteries, etc. BIS establishes and publishes specified standards in relation to products and certifies products meeting such standards with a certificate. This certification is voluntary unless directed by law or through an order of the government. The need for mandatory certification for EV batteries will largely depend upon the specification and the nature of chemicals and components used in the batteries.  
   Where certification is mandatory, the product manufacturer will have to ensure that the products comply with all the requirements and norms under the relevant standard to ensure that the product receives the certification. Even where the certification is voluntary, the product manufacturer can apply for certification after complying with the requisite standards.
6. **Which are the major policies of the Indian government to boost the EV market in India?**6.1 The National Electric Mobility Mission Plan, 2020 announced in 2012 lays down the roadmap for faster adoption of EVs and promotes domestic manufacturing of EVs. In 2015, the Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid &) Electric Vehicles in India’ (“FAME”) scheme was launched and proposed to be implemented in two phases which are discussed below:  
   6.2 FAME phase I – FAME phase I was launched on 13 March 2015 and INR 8.95 billion was budgeted towards subsidies to generate demand, build infrastructure and technology platforms. Thirty OEMs and one hundred thirty-seven models of all categories of vehicles registered under this phase to avail benefits such as subsidies.  
   6.3 FAME phase II – FAME phase II was launched on 01 April 2019 and INR 100 billion has been budgeted towards four key areas i.e., technology development, demand creation, pilot projects and charging infrastructure. FAME phase II gives prominence to domestic manufacturing of EVs, batteries and other components, with special emphasis on incentives to reduce battery cost, which was missing in FAME phase I. The budgetary outlay of INR 100 billion is proposed to be utilised within a period of 3 (three) years from 01 April 2019 and about 86% of the budgeted amount has been earmarked for providing demand incentives and 10% has been set aside for incentives towards creation of charging infrastructure.
7. **What State level policies have been implemented to boost adoption of EVs?**Several States have adopted individual polices providing fiscal and non-fiscal incentives for localized manufacturing and demand generation. Though the policies vary from state to state, they all share a common aim to develop a robust charging network and an integrated EV ecosystem. As of May 2021, 14 (fourteen) states have either approved and adopted or have drafted EV specific policies to boost EV adoption in their states, a summary of which is given in the table below:

| --- | --- | --- |
| **S. No.** | **State** | **Key initiatives** |
| 1 | Karnataka | Aims to achieve 100% e-mobility in auto-rickshaws, cab aggregators, corporate fleets, and school buses/vans by 2030.Introduction of 1,000 (one thousand) EV buses for local public transport.Provides incentives such as interest-free loans on the net state goods and service tax for EV manufacturing enterprises.Focuses on a venture capital fund for e-mobility start-ups, and the creation of a secondary market for batteries.Aims to set up over 100 (one hundred) EV charging stations in Bengaluru. |
| 2 | Maharashtra | Aims to increase the number of registered EVs to 500,000 (five hundred thousand).Exempts EVs from road tax and registration fees over five-year policy period.Enables fuel stations to set up charging points through governing regulations.Aims to provide support for EV public charging infrastructure by planning authorities and electricity supply agencies.Provides incentives for micro, small and medium enterprises and large manufacturing units engaged in the sector. |
| 3 | Andhra Pradesh | Aims to have one million EVs on the road by 2024.Aims to provide complete reimbursement of road tax and registration fees on sale of EVs until 2024.Aims to replace public transport buses in four cities to e-buses by 2024 and across the state by 2030.Aims to establish 100,000 (one hundred thousand) slow and fast charging stations by 2024. |

| 11 | Gujarat | Aims to have 100,000 (one hundred thousand) EVs on the road by 2022, which includes 80,000 (eighty thousand) 2-wheelers or scooters,14,000 (fourteen thousand) 3-wheelers, 4,500 (four thousand five hundred) cars, and 1,500 (fifteen hundred) buses.Aims to provide one hundred percent exemption from registration fee and 50% exemption from motor vehicle tax.Aims to provide 100% exemption from electricity duty for EV charging stations.Provides additional state-level subsidy to supplement the FAME phase II. |

8. **What are India’s plans for localizing the EV supply chain?**  
The Indian government has approved the ‘National Mission on Transformative Mobility and Energy Storage’ (“Mission”) which emphasizes on setting up a few large-scale, export-competitive, integrated batteries and cell-manufacturing giga factories i.e., huge battery manufacturing centers where lithium-ion batteries – the building blocks of EV batteries – are crafted. Recently, NITI Aayog proposed incentives worth INR 300 billion for setting up at least four giga factories by 2030. This includes initial capital assistance and infrastructure incentives worth INR 9 billion in 2021, which can be escalated annually.

9. **What are the policies regarding handling of waste associated with lithium-ion batteries?**  
The Indian government has published the draft Battery Waste Management Rules, 2020 which provides a blueprint of a cohesive set of rules tailor made for recycling and safe disposal of EV batteries. Under the said rules, the manufacturers and dealers of batteries will need to ensure that used batteries are sent only to the registered recyclers and that the environment is not harmed during their transportation. Therefore, the rules put the onus of collection of batteries and their safe transport to the recyclers, on the manufacturers and dealers.

# Karnataka’s next opportunity to boost the vehicle transition — a ZEV mandate

April 17, 2025 | By: Sumati Kohli

*This piece originally appeared in the* [Hindustan Times](https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/karnatakas-next-opportunity-to-boost-the-vehicle-transition-a-zev-mandate-101742802655818.html)*.*

Karnataka ranked [third among all states in India](https://www.autocarpro.in/analysis-sales/revealed-indias-top-15-states-uts-for-electric-2w-3w-pv-and-cv-sales-in-cy2024-124764) in total new battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales (two-wheelers, three-wheelers, passenger vehicles, and commercial vehicles) in calendar year 2024. That was enough for a [9% BEV sales share](https://vahan.parivahan.gov.in/vahan4dashboard/vahan/vahan/view/reportview.xhtml), higher than most states, and more than 5,700 new public charging stations were installed in Karnataka that year, the most of any state in the country. 

There’s more good news. The [Clean Mobility Policy 2025-30](https://industries.karnataka.gov.in/storage/pdf-files/8211.pdf) launched last month includes a special focus on developing the state’s manufacturing ecosystem for zero-emission vehicles, a term that includes BEVs and hydrogen fuel-cell electric vehicles (FCEVs). Already a major automobile manufacturing hub, Karnataka could, with the additional support from the policy, become a locus for innovation in clean automotive technologies and play a pivotal role in realising India’s ZEV transition goals. The new policy offers support across the ZEV value chain, from battery and cell manufacturing and recycling to charging infrastructure, hydrogen refuelling stations, and more. 

This comes in the form of incentives, including a capital investment subsidy, waiver of stamp duty, concessional registration charges, and reimbursement of the land-conversion fee. The policy also includes initiatives for developing the skills of the automotive workforce to align with the needs of the ZEV transition.

Governments in leading auto markets such as California and China supplement such incentives with supply-side regulations like sales mandates to ramp up ZEV adoption across segments. These mandates require manufacturers to sell a certain minimum percentage of ZEVs in their total vehicle sales over a period of time. California implemented [its ZEV mandate in 1990](https://theicct.org/publication/designing-a-zero-emission-vehicle-sales-regulation-for-2w-in-india-mar24/) and leads the United States in ZEV deployment, with a [market share of about three times](https://www.cncda.org/wp-content/uploads/Cal-Covering-4Q-24-FINAL.pdf) the American average.

There are key advantages to ZEV sales regulations. Prior [ICCT research](https://theicct.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ID-115-%E2%80%93-ZEV-mandate_paper_final.pdf) found that they could increase the number of ZEV model choices available, as manufacturers would increase their offerings to attract consumers. In the United States in 2023, [six of the top 10 states for passenger car electric vehicle](https://theicct.org/publication/ev-ldv-us-major-markets-monitor-2023-june24/) (EV) sales (EVs are BEVs, FCEVs, and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles) had deployed ZEV mandates, and these states were home to about 50% of the total EV sales in the country. 

Additionally, each of the six had more than 70 different EV models available on the market. A ZEV sales regulation would increase industry-wide manufacturing and lead to economies of scale that would ultimately bring down the purchase price of ZEVs. This would also be likely to expedite the achievement of cost parity with internal combustion engine vehicles. In practice, ZEV mandates are met by manufacturers either through ZEV sales or the purchase of surplus credits from other manufacturers that overachieved on their sales targets under the regulation. 

Manufacturers slow to embrace ZEVs could risk losing market competitiveness as they transition. A ZEV sales mandate also offers some certainty to ZEV refuelling infrastructure providers about the number of vehicles expected on the roads in the future, and this facilitates investment planning well in advance. 

In India, implementing ZEV sales regulations requires legal authority through legislation or judicial intervention. For instance, in 2015, [the Supreme Court directed](https://indianexpress.com/article/cities/delhi/supreme-court-ban-on-diesel-taxis-2781490/) that all taxis running in the National Capital Region be run on compressed natural gas by early 2016. Additionally, a well-established supporting institutional framework and coordination among key stakeholders is needed for successful implementation. The buildout of adequate charging infrastructure is crucial for scaling up ZEV deployment, and that will need coordination among and action from the government, DISCOMs, industry, and standardisation organisations. 

The alignment and support of industry bodies, technology and policy research organisations, government funding agencies, and financial institutions will also be needed for successful implementation of these regulations. Thus far, purchase and manufacturing incentives have been the driving force behind Karnataka’s ZEV transition. 

As the state forges ahead with its goal of becoming a ZEV manufacturing leader, supplementing these incentives with well-designed ZEV sales regulations can serve as a potent policy lever to accelerate the transition and bring benefits to both consumers and manufacturers.

# Identifying opportunities and bottlenecks

The Brookings India discussion in Bengaluru focused on three main threads: manufacturing, systems-level issues, and future unknowns and risks.

At a risk of over-simplification, there are three parts to an EV: the battery, the electronics and electrical systems, and the rest of the vehicle. India already has significant manufacturing skills and capacity for the rest of the vehicle. Batteries are a tough challenge since India today lacks the resources supply chain for specialised materials, including lithium and cobalt, and China is a world leader in this space, not necessarily based on state-of-the-art but on the scale of manufacturing. A competitive solution to this may take time to emerge. This leaves the electrical and electronics portion for innovation and scaling. One possible new option is the creation of modular platforms, which can separate the battery from other components, all of which could be mixed and matched. This has the additional benefit of allowing not just customisation but the possibility to achieve scale without necessarily having a single mega-sized facility. This could even allow for a larger number of small- to medium-scale factories across India.

Another challenge that needs to be addressed head-on is the lack of systems-level coordination. EVs aren’t just about manufacturing, and require, as a start, coordination with the grid.  Solutions like fast-charging, which reduce consumers’ range anxiety and can also allow cost savings through smaller battery packs, mean a higher stress on the grid. While the short-run impacts are likely to be manageable, long-term solutions will require time-of-day pricing to ensure synergy instead of conflict between EVs and the grid. There is also the related issue of when the EV plug in for charging, if it is during night times when coal-based power is available, it will be worse greenhouse gases-wise compared to internal combustion engines.

A lot of effort needs to focus on early adopters, especially fleet vehicles, as well as understanding future technologies and change. Much of tomorrow’s infrastructure is yet to be built and digital systems are growing rapidly. Transitioning from niche to mass-markets are a function of consumer preferences and availability of options that meet their needs and expectations.

Experience in ‘budget’ electric two-wheeler and car segments has shown how under-powered and lower range vehicles hurt long-run market growth as they don’t necessarily cater to the basic aspirations of the buyers. Financing of EVs is still a bottleneck as since they are a new item on the list of the book-keepers, their depreciation and residual value are not well established like conventional vehicles.

Such issues will resolve over time, and are second order to the broader challenge of providing a cost-effective and quality product with a reasonable payback period.
